- This is Boeing’s Form 10-K index for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2022, outlining Parts I–IV and standard SEC items: Business; Risk Factors; Properties; Legal Proceedings; Market for common equity and issuer repurchases; MD&A; Market Risk; Financial Statements and Supplementary Data; Changes in and Disagreements with Accountants; Controls and Procedures; Other Information; Disclosure regarding foreign jurisdictions that prevent inspections; Governance and Compensation items; Exhibits and Financial Statement Schedules; 10-K Summary; and Signatures.
- Item 1 (Business) begins with an overview of Boeing as a major global aerospace company organized into four reportable segments:
  - Commercial Airplanes (BCA): Develops, produces, and markets commercial jet aircraft. Current families include the 737 (narrow-body) and the 767, 777, and 787 (wide-body). Production of the 747 ended in 2022. Ongoing development includes the 777X and 737-7/737-10 derivatives.
  - Defense, Space & Security (BDS): Researches, develops, produces, and modifies manned/unmanned military aircraft and weapons systems for strike, surveillance, and mobility; fighter and trainer aircraft; vertical lift (rotorcraft and tilt-rotor); commercial derivative aircraft (e.g., anti-submarine, tanker). Also provides strategic defense and intelligence systems (missile defense, C4ISR, cyber, intelligence), satellite systems (government and commercial), and space exploration.
  - Global Services (BGS): Provides lifecycle services for commercial and defense customers, including supply chain/logistics, engineering, maintenance and modifications, upgrades/conversions, spare parts, pilot and maintenance training, technical documents, and data analytics/digital services.
  - Boeing Capital (BCC): Supports customer financing for Boeing products and manages financing exposure. Portfolio includes operating leases, finance leases, notes and other receivables, assets held for sale or re-lease, and investments.

structure.title: Business
structure.heading: Item 1. Business
structure.start_phrase: The Boeing Company, together with its subsidiaries (herein referred to as “Boeing,” the “Company,” “we,” “us,” “our”), is one of the world’s major aerospace firms.
structure.summary:
- Overview of The Boeing Company as a major aerospace firm and its organization into four reportable segments: Commercial Airplanes (BCA), Defense, Space & Security (BDS), Global Services (BGS), and Boeing Capital (BCC).
- Segment details:
  - BCA: Development, production, and marketing of commercial jetliners; current models include 737, 767, 777, 787; 747 production ended in 2022; ongoing development of 777X and 737-7/-10.
  - BDS: Research, development, production, and modification of manned/unmanned military aircraft, rotorcraft, commercial derivatives (e.g., tanker, anti-submarine), strategic defense and intelligence systems (C4ISR, cyber), satellites, and space exploration.
  - BGS: Global aftermarket services across the platform lifecycle (supply chain, logistics, maintenance, engineering, modifications, upgrades, training, technical documentation, analytics and digital services).
  - BCC: Customer financing to support Boeing product deliveries; portfolio includes leases, notes/receivables, assets held for sale or re-lease, and investments.
- Intellectual property: Extensive patent portfolio and licenses (including U.S. government licenses on government-funded inventions); trademarks, trade secrets, and know-how are important; no single IP right is critical to the business.
- Human capital:
  - Workforce of ~156,000 at Dec 31, 2022 (13% outside U.S.); ~142,000 in 2021.
  - Union representation (~50,000 employees): IAM (~20%, agreements expiring 2024/2025), SPEEA (~10%, expiring 2026), UAW (~1%, expiring 2027).
  - Commitment to diversity, equity, and inclusion; 2022 Global EDI report; as of Dec 2021 U.S. workforce ~23% women, 33% racial/ethnic minorities, 15% veterans; active Business Resource Groups.
  - Talent and engagement: Competitive benefits; 2022 voluntary resignation ~4%; ~23,000 hires with 78% offer acceptance; employee surveys and recognition programs.
  - Learning and development: ~5.8 million learning hours in 2022; tuition assistance with 300+ institutions; 9,000+ employees participating annually. Emphasis on safety, quality, integrity, sustainability, and annual Code of Conduct certification with multiple reporting channels.
- Competition:
  - BCA: Intense global competition (e.g., Airbus, Chinese entrants); focus on product/process improvement, cost reduction, safety, efficiency, and value.
  - BDS: Strong competitors (Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon Technologies, General Dynamics, SpaceX; BAE Systems and Airbus in U.S. market); teaming among competitors; competitive pressures expected to persist.
  - BGS: Highly competitive services market; growth targeted via customer satisfaction and productivity.
- Regulatory matters:
  - Engagement with U.S. agencies (DoD branches, NASA, FAA, DHS) and non-U.S. authorities.
  - Government contracts may be terminated for convenience or default with defined payment/liability outcomes.
  - FAA and international certification/regulatory compliance for commercial aircraft.
  - Environmental laws and potential climate-related costs; ongoing compliance and remediation efforts with potential material impact if standards tighten (reference to Note 13).
  - Non-U.S. sales subject to export controls, tariffs, anti-corruption, currency, political, and economic risks.
- Supply chain and materials:
  - Key materials: aluminum, titanium, composites; alternative source qualification can take a year or more.
  - Suspension of titanium purchases from Russia due to the Russia-Ukraine war; mitigated via inventory and alternative sources.
  - Reliance on many suppliers, including sole-source arrangements; supplier performance and energy availability are critical risks.
- Seasonality: No material seasonal effects.
- Corporate and investor information: Incorporation history (WA 1916; DE 1934); headquarters in Arlington, Virginia; website and SEC filings access; website content not incorporated by reference.
- Forward-looking statements: Cautionary language regarding expectations, assumptions, risks, uncertainties, and no obligation to update.
- Risk factors (excerpted):
  - Dependence on commercial airlines and exposure to cyclicality, macroeconomic conditions, financing availability, regulation, fuel prices, geopolitical events, and public health crises.
  - Backlog sensitivity to long-term market changes; potential for order deferrals/cancellations.
  - Fixed-price contracts with indexed escalation can impact revenues and margins if costs outpace indices.
  - Revenue concentration with a limited number of airlines; risks from customer fleet decisions, consolidations, or financial stress.

structure.title: Risk Factors
structure.heading: Item 1A. Risk Factors
structure.start_phrase: An investment in our common stock or debt securities involves risks and uncertainties and our actual results and future trends may differ materially from our past or projected future performance.
structure.summary:
- Forward-looking statements disclaimer outlining uncertainty and no obligation to update.
- Item 1A. Risk Factors:
  - Business and operations:
    - Heavy dependence on commercial airlines; exposure to cyclical demand, macroeconomics, financing availability, fuel prices, competition, geopolitical events, pandemics, and environmental regulations.
    - Pricing and cost risks from long-dated, fixed-price contracts with index-based escalation; potential margin impacts if costs outpace escalation.
    - Customer concentration risk; airline consolidations and financial stress may reduce orders or trigger cancellations/deferrals.
    - Inflationary pressures on airlines and the broader economy.
    - Production system and certification risks: need to maintain quality, meet rate targets, and achieve FAA and global regulatory approvals; impacts from evolving certification laws (e.g., ACSAA, 737-7 and 737-10 safety enhancements and retrofits).
    - Program-specific challenges and delays (737, 777X, 787), including supplier quality issues, inspections, rework, delivery suspensions, and related customer remedies.
    - Need to stabilize production, manage rate changes, improve productivity, and secure timely, cost-effective supplier deliveries; ongoing supply chain constraints, inflation, and labor instability.
    - Performance, reliability, and emerging sustainability requirements could increase costs or reduce revenues, especially for newer programs.
    - U.S. defense spending uncertainty: timing/levels of appropriations, continuing resolutions, shifting acquisition priorities (affordability, innovation, cybersecurity, data/software delivery), and NASA/other agency budgets.
    - Supplier and subcontractor performance and financial stability; raw material availability and pricing (aluminum, titanium, composites), single-source risks, and impacts from geopolitical events (e.g., suspension of Russian titanium).
    - Intense competition across commercial, defense, and services markets; international competitors and compliance requirements affecting cost competitiveness.
    - International sales risks (significant non-U.S. revenue): regulatory changes, trade disputes/tariffs, sourcing and offset rules, FX volatility, political/economic instability, financing availability (including Ex-Im), sanctions/embargoes; China market uncertainty (737 MAX deliveries) and Russia-Ukraine impacts.
    - Accounting estimates/program accounting risks: complex judgments on revenues, costs, accounting quantities, mix, escalation, supplier claims, certification timing; changes can materially affect results.
    - Mergers, acquisitions, joint ventures/alliances, and divestitures: integration, legacy liabilities, impairments, partner performance, and ongoing financial commitments.
  - Contracts:
    - U.S. government contracts subject to extensive procurement rules; potential cost increases from new requirements (e.g., domestic content, climate/cyber disclosures), withholds, penalties, or reduced business for noncompliance.
    - Risk of contract modification, curtailment, termination (for convenience or default), or funding reductions; appropriations uncertainty.
    - Audits, inquiries, and investigations can result in withholds, refunds, penalties, reputational harm, or debarment.
    - Fixed-price contracts (significant share of defense/services revenue): exposure to cost overruns, schedule/performance penalties, and reach-forward losses; heightened risk on complex development programs (e.g., Commercial Crew, KC-46A, MQ-25, T-7A, VC-25B, satellites).
    - Cost-type contracts: fee uncertainty, potential for lower margins or cancellation on complex programs (e.g., GMD, Proprietary, SLS).
    - In-orbit incentive payment exposure on satellite contracts; potential revenue reversals/refunds if performance falls short.
  - Cybersecurity and business disruptions:
    - Evolving cyber threats to IT systems, data, products, and supply chain; potential loss of IP, data breaches, operational disruption, and reputational/financial harm; reference to 2022 Jeppesen incident.
    - Disruptions from physical security threats, extreme weather/climate impacts, and pandemics affecting internal and supplier operations.
  - Legal and regulatory:
    - Litigation, inquiries, and investigations with unpredictable outcomes; potential material financial and reputational impacts.
    - Environmental liabilities from past/current operations and acquired entities; potential for increased costs due to new laws, enforcement, or discovered contamination.
    - Climate/ESG risks: regulatory and market transitions, stricter emissions and performance standards, disclosure requirements, supply chain impacts; risks to achieving public sustainability goals and related reputational/capital access implications.
  - Financing and liquidity:
    - Elevated debt levels and significant upcoming maturities; dependence on access to capital markets; sensitivity to credit ratings, market conditions, and airplane financing commitments.
    - Pension and other postretirement benefit obligations: volatility from discount rates, asset returns, medical costs; impacts on earnings, equity, cash flows, and contract profitability.
    - Potential inadequacy of insurance coverage for certain products/risks; limited protections outside the U.S.; exposure from major accidents.
    - Customer financing portfolio concentration by customer, region, and aircraft types (notably 717 and 747-8); redeployment and residual value risks.
  - Labor:
    - Significant unionized workforce; risk of strikes/work stoppages at the company or suppliers that could delay production, strain customer relationships, and reduce revenues.
- Item 1B. Unresolved Staff Comments: Not applicable.

structure.start_phrase:
We are a global market leader in the design, development, manufacture, sale, service and support of commercial jetliners, military aircraft,
satellites, missile defense, human space flight and launch systems and services.
structure.summary:
- Company overview and strategy, including core segments: Commercial Airplanes (BCA), Defense, Space & Security (BDS), Global Services (BGS), and Boeing Capital (BCC)
- Business environment and trends: post‑COVID commercial recovery (domestic ahead of international), supply chain disruptions, labor instability, inflation; airline profitability outlook (IATA); long-term demand forecast (20‑year CMO); strong freighter demand; BGS commercial recovery; stable BDS demand; impacts from the war in Ukraine and suspension of Russian operations
- Consolidated results (2020–2022): revenue growth to 2022, continued operating losses, non‑GAAP core metrics; segment revenue/margin drivers; unallocated items (share-based plans, deferred comp, R&D, SEC settlement, environmental); pension FAS/CAS effects; other income (non‑operating pension/postretirement), interest expense; minimal expected impact from the Inflation Reduction Act
- Costs and expenses: cost of sales trends and ratios; R&D spending by segment with 2022 increase (notably 777X, 737 MAX, enterprise investments)
- Backlog: total, contractual vs unobligated; increase driven by BCA; risks from potential delays (737 MAX China deliveries, 777X, 737‑7/‑10 entry into service)
- Global trade considerations: U.S.–China relations/tariffs; steel and aluminum tariffs; Russia sanctions and compliance; monitoring for supply chain/customer impacts
- Segment results and outlook:
  - Commercial Airplanes (BCA): competitive landscape (Airbus, COMAC); higher 2022 deliveries (737, 787) and revenue; reduced losses vs 2021; abnormal production costs; detailed program status:
    - 737: production at ~31/month; certification timelines for 737‑7 and 737‑10; inventory (including China-designated units) and delivery outlook; safety enhancement retrofit requirements
    - 747: production completed
    - 767: near break-even margins; combined rate ~3/month
    - 777/777X: revised 777X‑9 first delivery to 2025; production pause in 2022–2023 with ~$1.5B abnormal costs; launch of 777X‑8F for 2027; risk of further reach‑forward losses
    - 787: deliveries resumed in 2022; abnormal production costs estimate raised to ~$2.8B; low production rates with planned ramp; accounting quantity increased improving margins; customer considerations and rework
    - Program accounting quantities, deliveries, backlog dynamics, and development schedules
  - Defense, Space & Security (BDS): FY23 U.S. appropriations (DoD/NASA) and program funding; non‑U.S. opportunities; 2022 revenue decline and large fixed‑price development charges (VC‑25B, KC‑46A, MQ‑25, T‑7A, Commercial Crew); deliveries by platform; lower backlog; risks and potential for additional reach‑forward losses on complex fixed‑price programs
  - Global Services (BGS): market recovery to pre‑pandemic commercial volumes; competitive pressures; 2022 revenue/earnings growth driven by commercial services; lower government services (ended engine distribution agreement); backlog decline
  - Boeing Capital (BCC): small, concentrated portfolio with below‑investment‑grade exposure; limited 2022 funding; market context (parked fleet); lower revenues/earnings; balance sheet and intercompany mitigations
- Liquidity and capital resources:

nodes.title: Summary of Significant Accounting Policies
nodes.heading: Note 1 – Summary of Significant Accounting Policies
nodes.start_phrase: The Consolidated Financial Statements included in this report have been prepared by management of The Boeing Company (herein referred to as “Boeing,” the “Company,” “we,” “us” or “our”).
nodes.summary:
- Context: Notes to The Boeing Company’s Consolidated Financial Statements for years ended 2022, 2021, and 2020 (dollars in millions), covering significant accounting policies and selected note disclosures.

- Consolidation and segments: Financial statements include all majority-owned subsidiaries and required VIEs; intercompany eliminated. Four reportable segments: Commercial Airplanes (BCA), Defense, Space & Security (BDS), Global Services (BGS), and Boeing Capital (BCC).

- Use of estimates and operating cycle: Extensive management judgment under U.S. GAAP; contract/program duration used as operating cycle (often >1 year).

- Revenue recognition:
  - Commercial aircraft (BCA): Transaction price allocated to aircraft; revenue at point of delivery/acceptance; program accounting used for cost of sales; customer advances/progress payments not a significant financing component.
  - Long-term contracts (primarily BDS, some BGS): Typically a single performance obligation; revenue recognized over time via cost-to-complete (costs incurred plus proportionate profit); handles fixed-price and cost-reimbursable, with variable consideration; cumulative catch-up adjustments for estimate changes; recognize reach-forward losses when expected. 2022 saw large adverse adjustments (notably VC-25B, KC-46A, MQ-25, Commercial Crew, T-7A) that decreased revenue and increased operating loss.
  - Commercial spare parts (BGS): Point-in-time revenue at delivery; returns considered in transaction price; average cost for COGS.
  - Other services (BGS): Over-time recognition (e.g., maintenance, training, analytics) using methods best depicting transfer of control.
  - Concession sharing: Supplier reimbursements reduce cost of products.
  - Contract assets/liabilities: Unbilled receivables and advances/progress billings recorded by contract; generally not significant financing.

- Financial services revenue (BCC and related activities): Accounting for sales-type/direct finance and operating leases; recognition of selling profit, interest income, non-accrual policies, residual value reviews, impairments, and operating lease depreciation; impairment and asset-held-for-sale treatment.

- Reinsurance: Astro Ltd. participates in a workers’ compensation reinsurance pool; revenues and costs presented net in cost of sales with amounts disclosed for 2020–2022.

- Research and development: Expensed as incurred unless tied to certain contracts; “best efforts” arrangements offset R&D expense; disclosure of bid and proposal costs.

- Share-based compensation: Equity awards measured at grant-date fair value; cash-settled awards remeasured each period; expense recognized over vesting net of estimated forfeitures.

- Income taxes: Provision based on current law; uncertain tax positions under more-likely-than-not threshold; valuation allowance assessments; interest/penalties in income tax line.

- Postretirement and postemployment: Defined benefit pension/OPEB accounting (assumptions, gains/losses in equity and amortization policy, funded status on balance sheet); liabilities for severance/job training when probable and estimable.

- Environmental remediation: Accruals when probable and estimable; undiscounted; potential recoveries recognized when probable.

- Cash and cash equivalents: Definition and bank set-off presentation (negative balances reclassified to accounts payable with disclosed amounts).

- Inventories and program accounting:
  - Components include engineering, production, tooling, overhead; abnormal or non-attributable fixed costs expensed.
  - Commercial program inventories include deferred production costs (to be recovered via average program margins) and supplier advances; NRV assessments via quarterly reviews.
  - Loss provisions recognized for long-term contracts and for commercial programs when estimated costs exceed revenues for remaining units.
  - Spare parts at lower of average cost or NRV; excess/obsolete write-downs; early issue sales consideration recorded as revenue reduction at delivery and assessed for recoverability.

- Precontract costs: Capitalized if probable of recovery; otherwise expensed/written off.

- Property, plant and equipment and leases (as lessee):
  - Useful lives and depreciation methods; capitalization and amortization of internal-use software and SaaS; impairment and held-for-sale rules.
  - Lease accounting for operating and finance leases: ROU assets and liabilities measured at PV of lease payments using incremental borrowing rate; variable payments expensed; options included when reasonably certain; real estate lease and non-lease components combined.

- Asset retirement obligations: Recorded when fair value reasonably estimable; conditional AROs recorded when estimable; some unknown obligations may exist.

- Goodwill and intangible assets (policies): Annual impairment testing (April 1) using qualitative/quantitative methods; indefinite-lived assets (trade names, IPR&D) tested against discounted cash flows; finite-lived intangibles amortized over defined lives with impairment testing on indicators.

- Investments: Time deposits at cost; AFS debt securities at fair value with OCI; equity method for significant influence; other equity at fair value or cost minus impairment; operating vs non-operating investment income presentation.

- Derivatives: All at fair value; cash flow hedges through OCI to earnings; aluminum purchase/sale and other economic hedges not designated—changes go to earnings.

- Credit loss allowances: Quarterly assessment across receivables and certain financial assets using credit ratings, default data, aging, expected loss rates, and collateral; collateral values from third-party aircraft publications with judgment as needed; some cross-collateralization rights.

- Commercial aircraft trade-in commitments: Potential revenue adjustments at delivery and/or COGS charges for value declines between contract and trade-in; fair value based on aircraft-specific and market data with quarterly updates.

- Warranties and performance guarantees: Standard warranty terms for BCA and BDS; accruals based on coverage periods and historical claims plus specific major issues; aircraft performance guarantees treated as warranties; supplier recoveries recognized.

- Supplier penalties and guarantees: Accrue supplier penalties when probable/estimable; recognize fair value of guarantees at inception and update expected losses.

- Note 2 – Goodwill and acquired intangibles:
  - Goodwill by segment with minor adjustments; total goodwill of $8,057 at Dec 31, 2022.
  - Indefinite-lived intangibles: $197 trade names; $202 IPR&D for a next-generation air vehicle.
  - Finite-lived intangibles: Categories, accumulated amortization; 2020 impairment of $178 on distribution rights; amortization expense of $241 (2022) and $284 (2021); expected amortization for 2023–2027 disclosed.

- Note 3 – Earnings per share: EPS computed using the two-class method, allocating undistributed earnings between common shares and participating securities.

- Exhibit 10.13: The Boeing Company Executive Supplemental Savings Plan (amended and restated Dec 21, 2022; effective Jan 1, 2022)
  - Overview and status: a nonqualified, unfunded deferred compensation “top-hat” plan with an excess benefit component; integrates the prior Deferred Compensation Plan (DCP) as of 2022.
  - Four components:
    1) Extra Deferrals (voluntary deferrals of base pay, cash incentives, and vested performance awards);
    2) Restoration Benefit (restores 401(k) benefits limited by IRC §§415 and 401(a)(17));
    3) Executive Benefit (Company Non-Elective Contributions and DC SERP Contributions; legacy Executive SSP+ noted);
    4) DCP Accounts (from the merged, frozen DCP).
  - Key definitions: eligibility; accounts and sub-accounts; contribution types (Restoration Matching, Restoration True-Up, Incentive Matching, Company Non-Elective, DC SERP); Cash Incentive; Performance Awards; Specified Employee; Separation from Service.
  - Participant deferrals: eligibility and election windows; limits (up to 50% base pay; 100% cash incentive and vested performance awards); mid-year rules for newly eligible employees; 409A-compliant timing/irrevocability; emergency cancellation for Unforeseeable Emergency.
  - Company contributions:
    - Restoration Matching tied to 401(k) match formula for Restoration Deferrals.
    - Restoration True-Up to mirror 401(k) true-up within limits and employment conditions.
    - Incentive Matching on Cash Incentive Deferrals (no match post-termination).
    - Company Non-Elective Contributions (e.g., 2% of base pay and cash incentive for 2022–2023, subject to service/termination conditions).
    - DC SERP Contributions: eligibility cohorts (hired 2009–2019 vs. pre-2009; excludes elected officers and post-1/1/2020 hires/promotions); ongoing payroll-based credits by level; a one-time promotion-based contribution; detailed service counting rules (including ULA/USA transfers).
  - Vesting/forfeiture:
    - Extra and Restoration accounts: 100% vested.
    - Executive Benefit: generally vested; legacy Executive SSP+ subject to misconduct/competition/confidentiality forfeiture and clawback.
    - DC SERP: complex vesting (36 consecutive months at executive level, death, eligible layoff; special 55/10 or 62/1 rules; treatment of absences/transfers); separate component vesting; misconduct/competition/confidentiality forfeiture and clawback provisions.
  - Distributions:
    - Elections for Extra Deferral and Restoration accounts (lump sum or 2–15 annual installments) with default to lump sum after Separation; Executive Benefit defaults to lump sum after Separation.
    - 409A-compliant change rules (one-time, 12-month advance, 5-year re-deferral); mandatory start by Jan following the later of age 70½ and Separation; six-month delay for Specified Employees; hardship withdrawals for Unforeseeable Emergency (not for DC SERP); beneficiary payouts and rehire/authorized absence payment coordination; small-balance cash-out at ≤$10,000.
  - Accounts and earnings: recordkeeping by employment period; earnings crediting via Interest Fund (Moody’s AA industrial yield-based rate), Boeing Stock Fund (unitized, non-equity), and other 401(k)-like investment options; daily transfer rules and Boeing Stock Fund 30-day roundtrip restriction; handling of missing participants and improper credits.
  - Administration and claims: administered by the Employee Benefit Plans Committee; claims procedures aligned with Boeing 401(k); Compensation Committee reviews elected officer appeals (except forfeiture determinations).
  - Amendment/termination: authority of Board, Compensation Committee, and Administrator; preservation of accrued benefits; 409A-compliant plan termination option.
  - Miscellaneous: no employment rights; anti-assignment; unfunded/rabbi trust status; 409A compliance (delays/accelerations, involuntary inclusion distribution); governing law (Illinois) and venue; tax withholding incl. FICA pyramiding; employing entity liability for payments; recovery of overpayments; notice procedures.
  - Appendices: A (excluded entities—reserved); B (legacy DCP rules on forfeiture/reinstatement of match, diversification eligibility, separate distribution elections, and rehire coordination).
